overview: The Modified Binary Search pattern is an algorithmic framework that adapts the classic binary search technique to locate elements, bounds, or transition thresholds in structured datasets. While traditional binary search targets specific values in fully sorted arrays, this modified pattern solves advanced variations such as searching order-agnostic ranges, circular letters, infinite data streams, bitonic structures, and rotated sorted arrays. By iteratively bisecting the search space, it maintains a logarithmic $O(\log N)$ runtime and constant $O(1)$ auxiliary space complexity.
recognition_signals: Sorted Inputs: The collection is an array, list, or matrix sorted ascending, descending, or circularly.
Rotated/Mountain Arrays: The array is sorted but rotated around a pivot, or rises and then falls (bitonic/mountain array).
Unknown Size Streams: The size of the dataset is not defined or is infinite.
Logarithmic Time Bounds: The problem requires a runtime of $O(\log N)$ or better.
In-Place Space Limits: The problem mandates $O(1)$ constant space, forbidding heap allocations or tracking tables.
Ceiling, Floor, or Range Search: Finding the closest smaller/larger elements, or range limits (`first` and `last` occurrence indices).

mental_model.analogy: Imagine playing a high-low number guessing game or searching for a name in a physical alphabetical phonebook.
mental_model.description:
Imagine playing a **high-low number guessing game** or searching for a name in a physical **alphabetical phonebook**.

If you are guessing a number between $1$ and $100$ and your guess of $50$ is "too low," you do not guess $51, 52, 53$ one by one. You immediately jump to $75$, discarding the lower half of the remaining range. For rotated or bitonic arrays, imagine opening the phonebook and realizing some pages are printed upside down or out of order. You first evaluate a page in the middle to identify which part is ordered, then perform your high-low bisection within the valid bounds.

brute_force_journey.brute_force_description: The brute force approach to searching or finding boundaries (like ceiling or minimum difference) is a linear scan from index `0` to `N-1`.
brute_force_journey.inefficiency_observation: Overlapping subsegments perform duplicate evaluations of identical elements.
brute_force_journey.optimization_concept:
```
  Brute Force
  [Scan the array linearly to find targets or boundaries -> O(N)]
       ↓
  Observation
  [The array exhibits sorted, bitonic, or rotated properties; we can determine sorting direction]
       ↓
  Optimization
  [Use Left/Right boundary pointers to calculate a mid-point and split the search range]
       ↓
  Final Pattern
  [Logarithmic bisection using index adjustments to target the valid partition in O(log N)]
```

---

animation_steps.description: Set left pointer = 0, right pointer = 6. Midpoint = 3 (value 8). Target = 10.
Target (10) > Midpoint (8). Shift left boundary to index 4. New mid = 5 (value 12).
Target (10) < Midpoint (12). Shift right boundary to index 4. New mid = 4 (value 10). Target found!

variants.name: **Order-Agnostic**
variants.description: `while (start <= end)` (Ascending vs descending check using start/end comparison.)

variants.name: **Ceiling / Floor**
variants.description: `while (start <= end)` (Exit loop and return `start` index (Ceiling) or `end` index (Floor).)

variants.name: **Circular Next**
variants.description: `while (start <= end)` (Ignore equality; return `start % length` to wrap around.)

variants.name: **Infinite Search**
variants.description: Exponential range search (First double range bounds ($1 \rightarrow 2 \rightarrow 4 \rightarrow 8$) then binary search.)

variants.name: **Rotated Search**
variants.description: `while (start <= end)` (Check which half is sorted, then query boundary containment.)

common_mistakes.description: **Integer Overflow:** Writing `(start + end) / 2` instead of `start + (end - start) / 2`. In languages with bounded integers (like C++ or Java), this can overflow and throw out-of-bounds exceptions.
**Infinite Loops:** Forgetting to shift pointers past the midpoint (`end = mid` instead of `end = mid - 1` in standard arrays), which stalls the search when `start == end`.
**Off-by-One Loop Terminations:** Incorrectly choosing `while (start < end)` for standard search instead of `while (start <= end)`, which fails to inspect the final single-element case.
**Duplicate Traps in Rotated Arrays:** Failing to handle cases where `arr[start] == arr[mid] == arr[end]`, leading to incorrect sorting-side decisions.

interview_perspective: Highly popular in FAANG/HFT rounds testing optimized traversals.

cheat_sheet: Always check for the overflow overflow-safe midpoint.

If you get stuck on rotated arrays, remember that at least one half of a rotated array is always sorted. Check `arr[start] <= arr[mid]` to confirm if the left half is sorted, and adjust bounds. When duplicate numbers exist, shift boundaries sequentially `start++, end--` only when start, mid, and end match.
